frase_gancho.texto: A building that already tells its story before you step inside.

puente_narrativo.texto: Cross the threshold. In the lobby, right in front of you, a mural more than twelve meters long gives you a preview, through two animals, of what you will find in the halls.

guion_corto.texto: Before going in, stop and take a look at the façade. Outside, you are greeted by a sober façade of Santo Tomás marble, with the National Coat of Arms carved in relief by José Chávez Morado; and as you cross toward the Central Courtyard, the second floor of the halls appears wrapped in a great geometric aluminum mesh: the lattice designed by Manuel Felguérez, inspired by the stepped-fret designs of Uxmal. Its pattern repeats a geometric shape that recalls the undulating body of a serpent, and the light from Chapultepec Forest passes through it and draws shadows that move throughout the day. President Adolfo López Mateos inaugurated this building on September 17, 1964, and its architect, Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, had one goal: for the museum to look like one more piece of the collection, a mid-twentieth-century building inspired by designs more than a thousand years old.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine a museum that was merely a warehouse of antiquities. Ramírez Vázquez thought the opposite: a building that would feel like an ancient city, with plazas, courtyards and a great central space, as in Uxmal or in Teotihuacán. That is why, from the outside, the museum does not ask your permission: it welcomes you with scale, with silence and with an underlying question, the question of what it means to belong to this country.

The construction was a race. President López Mateos commissioned the new museum in 1963, to move the collections out of the old building on Moneda Street, in the Centro, and everything had to be ready in less than two years. There were bricklayers, stonecutters, sculptors and artists working at the same time, and the result opened to the public in September 1964, nineteen months after work began.

Its architect, by the way, is an immense figure in the recent history of Mexico. Pedro Ramírez Vázquez also designed the new Basilica of Guadalupe, took part in the design of the Estadio Azteca and chaired the organizing committee of the 1968 Olympic Games. But none of those works had the task of this museum: to give a worthy home to the memory of an entire country.

Now take a look at the lattice, because it is the most ingenious piece of the façade. Manuel Felguérez, a sculptor and painter from Zacatecas and a pioneer of abstract art in Mexico, was inspired by the Puuc style of Uxmal, and especially by the friezes of the Nunnery Quadrangle, where the Maya assembled enormous stone mosaics with geometric forms. Felguérez took that idea and rewrote it in aluminum. It is a nod between two worlds: twentieth-century industrial technique dressed in the language of stone from more than a thousand years ago.

The lattice is not only beautiful; it works. It serves as a sunshade: it filters the sun and protects from the heat the halls on the upper floor, where the collections of today’s Indigenous peoples live. Below, the archaeological past; above, the living present; and between them, a mesh that joins the two times. Today this building is one of the most visited museums in Latin America, and almost all of its visitors walk beneath that pattern without noticing it. Not you, not anymore.

And the National Coat of Arms at the entrance is not there by chance. It is the image that springs from the founding of Tenochtitlan, the eagle on a prickly pear cactus devouring a serpent. When you reach the Mexica Hall, you will find that same scene carved in stone, on the back of the [Teocalli of the Sacred War](mna_s06_teocalli_guerra_sagrada), with a surprising detail: from its beak comes not a serpent, but a symbol of war.

One last fact for when you leave: this land has a memory of its own, and the museum stands within Chapultepec Forest, one of the great parks of the city. Chapultepec means “on the hill of the grasshopper,” and it was a sacred place and a source of water for the Mexica. The museum chose to stay right there.

texto: Look in the lattice for the modules that repeat: they look like the body of a serpent
Find the National Coat of Arms in relief above the entrance
Notice how the shadows of the aluminum change over the courtyard depending on the time of day

texto.Culture: Modern Mexican architecture: Pedro Ramírez Vázquez (architectural design), Manuel Felguérez (aluminum lattice of the Central Courtyard) and José Chávez Morado (National Coat of Arms in marble on the main façade)
texto.Material: Santo Tomás marble, glass and anodized aluminum lattice

texto.pregunta: Myth: The museum’s lattice is just a modern decoration with no connection to ancient Mexico.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is inspired by the stone walls of Uxmal and, in addition, serves as a sunshade for the halls on the upper floor.
